title: When physicians and AI work together, who is accountable? How to lay out medical liability
excerpt: A staging system based on how big a role AI has in patient care can help to identify who is responsible in cases in which care fails.
content_html:
Artificial intelligence is fast becoming embedded in hospitals and healthcare clinics. Yet, with the benefits of AI tools come fresh patient-safety risks — and questions about who is responsible when things go wrong.

Conventionally, responsibilities in health care are clearly delineated. Clinicians must provide a set standard of treatment. Institutions must organize safe treatment processes. Manufacturers must deliver non-defective medical devices. Regulators and bodies involved with licensing and credentials can intervene if any of these parties fall short of expected standards. And courts can assess which party is liable if patients are harmed.

An incoming wave of medical AI tools is set to blur these lines.

Current AI tools are being used mainly as assistants, backed up by human checks, much as with other medical devices. For instance, when AI models trigger an alert that a patient is at risk of sepsis, a clinician must review and confirm the physiological rationale before any treatment.

Medical AI can transform medicine — but only if we carefully track the data it touches

But in the next few years, AI-driven clinical tools are expected to advance from synthesizing data to acting on it, with less and less human input. They will make diagnoses, devise treatment plans and make patient-management decisions that clinicians play little or no part in. Whereas the outputs of many existing tools are understandable — sepsis models, for instance, work by combining defined physiological variables according to a transparent formula1 — more-advanced tools can involve black-box deep-learning processes. Clinicians will no longer be able to fully follow the tools’ reasoning, even for algorithms that provide some explanations for their judgements2.

Such tools land between accountability rules. Their black-box reasoning makes it hard to determine when they are defective. And when decisions are made jointly by humans and an opaque AI model, it becomes difficult to assess responsibility when people are harmed while receiving health care. Existing medical-liability frameworks do not address this crossover point3.

This legal uncertainty means that people who are harmed could fall into liability gaps in which no one has clearly broken a rule3. Hospitals are likely to avoid AI for potentially useful functions because of concerns about legal risks — concerns that are repeatedly cited by physicians as a barrier to safe AI adoption4–6 and that are seen by some as grounds not to use black-box tools already available. And AI vendors might shirk their obligation to monitor safety once a tool reaches the market, confident that it will be hard to attribute blame when things go wrong.

Clear liability frameworks are needed.

Here we outline how to achieve that, by defining seven levels of AI capabilities on the basis of three factors: autonomy, automation and operational scope. With aircraft and self-driving cars, regulators already use graded levels to specify exactly what tasks systems must perform, how independently, and when humans are expected to take over7–9. A similar set of levels for medical AI systems would help regulators, policymakers, governments, courts and professional health-care bodies to plan for the incoming tools.

Three properties, seven levels

Three properties dictate how AI is used in the clinic.

First, autonomy: how independently the system reasons, without the need for human input. Existing sepsis risk models are low-autonomy AI tools1. Deep-learning systems, by contrast, might arrive at diagnoses from patterns across thousands of variables, making inferences that physicians cannot retrace10.

Second, automation: what tasks a medical AI system can execute on its own. Such a system might range from a low-automation robot that a surgeon controls, to a system that sends chemotherapy prescriptions directly to a pharmacy.

Third, operational scope: the boundaries in which the system is allowed to run. A retinal-imaging system deployed by a specialist ophthalmology service to double-check clinical decisions is less risky than the same tool used in a primary-care clinic to make an autonomous decision about whether to refer a patient to a specialist.

The following seven levels could form a basis for defining risks around medical AI tools. A given tool might sit at different levels depending on where and how it is used, and by whom.

Level 0: Informational. An AI system with no autonomy, variable automation and narrow operational scope. Such systems store, move and display data according to rules set by humans. Examples include algorithms for managing electronic health records or streaming data from wearable devices that track vital signs. Algorithmic behaviour is transparent and any output is independently verifiable.

This is well-trodden ground. Regulators can assess whether such tools are reliable and offer sufficient cybersecurity and data protection. Courts can apply conventional standards to assess liability.

Level 1: Assistive. AI systems with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and narrow operational scope. Such systems can perform a single, clearly defined task, overseen by a clinician — such as flagging suspicious rhythms on a heart monitor11 or highlighting possible lung nodules on a scan12. The tools’ algorithmic reasoning might be opaque, but the output can be verified through clinical review of patient data, or by ‘explainability techniques’ that check correlations between the model’s input and output data.

These tools are regulated as diagnostic aids, similar to existing computer-aided detection systems for mammography and colonoscopy. Hospitals are held responsible for ensuring that staff understand their limitations. Users are expected to accurately judge whether alerts are meaningful.

Train clinical AI to reason like a team of doctors

Level 2: Decision support. AI tools with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and moderate operational scope. These systems combine multiple streams of data — perhaps including symptoms, previous medical history, imaging data and current guidelines. Existing tools at this level can produce a diagnosis and treatment plan, draft detailed discharge summaries and generate risk scores for triage decisions. As with level 1 tools, they are designed to be advisory — their reasoning might be opaque but is verifiable to some extent, and clinicians are expected to make the final decision.

Regulators should ask for robust evidence that these systems improve care. Hospitals must train clinicians to challenge outputs instead of accepting them by default, and courts must decide whether a clinician’s reliance on a particular recommendation was reasonable in the circumstances. There’s a risk that clinicians under time pressure will over-rely on advisory tools. There will be no easy way to determine how much a clinician was swayed by a machine’s recommendation.

Level 3: Supervised automation. AI systems with moderate levels of autonomy and automation, and moderate operational scope. The system, rather than the clinician, is the decision maker. These tools are currently rare (see ‘Classifying current medical AI’). In a tightly defined domain, they can dynamically respond to treatment needs — for example, devices for insulin delivery automatically adjust doses according to continuous glucose readings, using embedded algorithms and predefined limits13. The clinician selects which patients are placed on the system and intervenes only when something seems wrong.

Regulators should focus on the quality of instructions for using and maintaining these systems and on information about the risks inherent in providing care. Health-care organizations should furnish guidance for informed-consent protocols that respond to the new types of risk inherent in AI-driven treatment, and providers should discuss these risks with patients.

With these systems, physicians can be criticised for enrolling an unsuitable patient, failing to respond to device alarms or not understanding system limitations. Organizations might be judged on how they selected, validated and monitored the technology. Manufacturers might be liable if flawed designs or updates contribute to harm. But conventional liability assessments can be unfit for purpose, if physicians and organizations acted reasonably, and harm is caused by an algorithmically determined decision that is not obviously wrong.

Level 4: AI-triggered human oversight. AI tools with moderate-to-high levels of autonomy and automation, and broad operational scope. These systems manage whole episodes of therapy in areas such as intensive care. They continuously monitor patients and adjust treatments — for instance balancing ventilator and sedation settings against several physiological targets at once. They trigger back-up protocols such as summoning a rapid-response team when something seems wrong. Clinicians are a safety net and act only when the system sounds the alarm. Level 4 deployments are yet to break through in medicine, although the technical components needed are emerging.

For these systems, regulators should require strong evidence that including a human in the loop would reduce safety. Given that clinicians would have no realistic opportunity to review the actions of these systems, courts might struggle to determine whether an adverse outcome reflects negligence, a hidden defect or simply the inherent risks of medicine.

Generative AI could revolutionize health care — but not if control is ceded to big tech

sentences.zh: 以下七个级别可以构成定义医疗人工智能工具风险的基础。

sentences.en: A given tool might sit at different levels depending on where and how it is used, and by whom.
sentences.zh: 给定的工具可能处于不同的级别，具体取决于它的使用地点、方式以及使用者。

blocks.html_en: Level 0: Informational. An AI system with no autonomy, variable automation and narrow operational scope. Such systems store, move and display data according to rules set by humans. Examples include algorithms for managing electronic health records or streaming data from wearable devices that track vital signs. Algorithmic behaviour is transparent and any output is independently verifiable.

sentences.en: Level 0: Informational.
sentences.zh: 0 级：信息性。

sentences.en: An AI system with no autonomy, variable automation and narrow operational scope.
sentences.zh: 没有自主性、自动化程度可变、操作范围狭窄的人工智能系统。

sentences.en: Such systems store, move and display data according to rules set by humans.
sentences.zh: 此类系统根据人类设定的规则存储、移动和显示数据。

sentences.en: Examples include algorithms for managing electronic health records or streaming data from wearable devices that track vital signs.
sentences.zh: 例子包括管理电子健康记录的算法或来自跟踪生命体征的可穿戴设备的流数据。

sentences.en: Algorithmic behaviour is transparent and any output is independently verifiable.
sentences.zh: 算法行为是透明的，任何输出都是可独立验证的。

blocks.html_en: This is well-trodden ground. Regulators can assess whether such tools are reliable and offer sufficient cybersecurity and data protection. Courts can apply conventional standards to assess liability.

sentences.en: This is well-trodden ground.
sentences.zh: 这是人们常去的地方。

sentences.en: Regulators can assess whether such tools are reliable and offer sufficient cybersecurity and data protection.
sentences.zh: 监管机构可以评估此​​类工具是否可靠并提供足够的网络安全和数据保护。

sentences.en: Courts can apply conventional standards to assess liability.
sentences.zh: 法院可以应用传统标准来评估责任。

blocks.html_en: Level 1: Assistive. AI systems with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and narrow operational scope. Such systems can perform a single, clearly defined task, overseen by a clinician — such as flagging suspicious rhythms on a heart monitor11 or highlighting possible lung nodules on a scan12. The tools’ algorithmic reasoning might be opaque, but the output can be verified through clinical review of patient data, or by ‘explainability techniques’ that check correlations between the model’s input and output data.

sentences.en: Level 1: Assistive.
sentences.zh: 1 级：辅助。

sentences.en: AI systems with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and narrow operational scope.
sentences.zh: 自主性低、自动化程度低到中等、操作范围窄的人工智能系统。

sentences.en: Such systems can perform a single, clearly defined task, overseen by a clinician — such as flagging suspicious rhythms on a heart monitor11 or highlighting possible lung nodules on a scan12.
sentences.zh: 此类系统可以在临床医生的监督下执行单一、明确定义的任务，例如在心脏监护仪上标记可疑心律11或在扫描上突出显示可能的肺结节12。

sentences.en: The tools’ algorithmic reasoning might be opaque, but the output can be verified through clinical review of patient data, or by ‘explainability techniques’ that check correlations between the model’s input and output data.
sentences.zh: 这些工具的算法推理可能是不透明的，但可以通过对患者数据的临床审查或通过检查模型输入和输出数据之间的相关性的“可解释性技术”来验证输出。

blocks.html_en: These tools are regulated as diagnostic aids, similar to existing computer-aided detection systems for mammography and colonoscopy. Hospitals are held responsible for ensuring that staff understand their limitations. Users are expected to accurately judge whether alerts are meaningful.

sentences.en: These tools are regulated as diagnostic aids, similar to existing computer-aided detection systems for mammography and colonoscopy.
sentences.zh: 这些工具作为诊断辅助工具受到监管，类似于现有的乳房X光检查和结肠镜检查计算机辅助检测系统。

sentences.en: Hospitals are held responsible for ensuring that staff understand their limitations.
sentences.zh: 医院有责任确保工作人员了解其局限性。

sentences.en: Users are expected to accurately judge whether alerts are meaningful.
sentences.zh: 用户应该准确判断警报是否有意义。

blocks.html_en: Train clinical AI to reason like a team of doctors

sentences.en: Train clinical AI to reason like a team of doctors
sentences.zh: 训练临床人工智能像医生团队一样进行推理

blocks.html_en: Level 2: Decision support. AI tools with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and moderate operational scope. These systems combine multiple streams of data — perhaps including symptoms, previous medical history, imaging data and current guidelines. Existing tools at this level can produce a diagnosis and treatment plan, draft detailed discharge summaries and generate risk scores for triage decisions. As with level 1 tools, they are designed to be advisory — their reasoning might be opaque but is verifiable to some extent, and clinicians are expected to make the final decision.

sentences.en: Level 2: Decision support.
sentences.zh: 第 2 级：决策支持。

sentences.en: AI tools with low autonomy, low-to-moderate automation and moderate operational scope.
sentences.zh: 自主性低、自动化程度低到中等、操作范围适中的人工智能工具。

sentences.en: These systems combine multiple streams of data — perhaps including symptoms, previous medical history, imaging data and current guidelines.
sentences.zh: 这些系统结合了多个数据流——可能包括症状、既往病史、影像数据和当前指南。

sentences.en: Existing tools at this level can produce a diagnosis and treatment plan, draft detailed discharge summaries and generate risk scores for triage decisions.
sentences.zh: 此级别的现有工具可以制定诊断和治疗计划，起草详细的出院摘要并生成分诊决策的风险评分。

sentences.en: As with level 1 tools, they are designed to be advisory — their reasoning might be opaque but is verifiable to some extent, and clinicians are expected to make the final decision.
sentences.zh: 与 1 级工具一样，它们被设计为咨询性的——它们的推理可能不透明，但在某种程度上是可验证的，临床医生应该做出最终决定。

blocks.html_en: Regulators should ask for robust evidence that these systems improve care. Hospitals must train clinicians to challenge outputs instead of accepting them by default, and courts must decide whether a clinician’s reliance on a particular recommendation was reasonable in the circumstances. There’s a risk that clinicians under time pressure will over-rely on advisory tools. There will be no easy way to determine how much a clinician was swayed by a machine’s recommendation.

sentences.en: Regulators should ask for robust evidence that these systems improve care.
sentences.zh: 监管机构应要求提供强有力的证据来证明这些系统改善了护理。

sentences.en: Hospitals must train clinicians to challenge outputs instead of accepting them by default, and courts must decide whether a clinician’s reliance on a particular recommendation was reasonable in the circumstances.
sentences.zh: 医院必须培训临床医生质疑输出结果，而不是默认接受它们，法院必须决定临床医生在这种情况下对特定建议的依赖是否合理。

sentences.en: There’s a risk that clinicians under time pressure will over-rely on advisory tools.
sentences.zh: 临床医生在时间压力下可能会过度依赖咨询工具。

sentences.en: There will be no easy way to determine how much a clinician was swayed by a machine’s recommendation.
sentences.zh: 没有简单的方法可以确定临床医生在多大程度上受到机器建议的影响。

blocks.html_en: Level 3: Supervised automation. AI systems with moderate levels of autonomy and automation, and moderate operational scope. The system, rather than the clinician, is the decision maker. These tools are currently rare (see ‘Classifying current medical AI’). In a tightly defined domain, they can dynamically respond to treatment needs — for example, devices for insulin delivery automatically adjust doses according to continuous glucose readings, using embedded algorithms and predefined limits13. The clinician selects which patients are placed on the system and intervenes only when something seems wrong.

sentences.en: Level 3: Supervised automation.
sentences.zh: 第 3 级：监督自动化。

sentences.en: AI systems with moderate levels of autonomy and automation, and moderate operational scope.
sentences.zh: 具有中等自主性和自动化水平、中等操作范围的人工智能系统。

sentences.en: The system, rather than the clinician, is the decision maker.
sentences.zh: 决策者是系统，而不是临床医生。

sentences.en: These tools are currently rare (see ‘Classifying current medical AI’).
sentences.zh: 这些工具目前很少见（参见“当前医疗人工智能的分类”）。

sentences.en: In a tightly defined domain, they can dynamically respond to treatment needs — for example, devices for insulin delivery automatically adjust doses according to continuous glucose readings, using embedded algorithms and predefined limits13.
sentences.zh: 在严格定义的领域中，它们可以动态响应治疗需求 - 例如，胰岛素输送设备使用嵌入式算法和预定义的限制，根据连续血糖读数自动调整剂量13。

sentences.en: The clinician selects which patients are placed on the system and intervenes only when something seems wrong.
sentences.zh: 临床医生选择将哪些患者置于系统中，并仅在出现问题时进行干预。

blocks.html_en: Regulators should focus on the quality of instructions for using and maintaining these systems and on information about the risks inherent in providing care. Health-care organizations should furnish guidance for informed-consent protocols that respond to the new types of risk inherent in AI-driven treatment, and providers should discuss these risks with patients.

sentences.en: Regulators should focus on the quality of instructions for using and maintaining these systems and on information about the risks inherent in providing care.
sentences.zh: 监管机构应重点关注使用和维护这些系统的说明的质量以及有关提供护理所固有风险的信息。

sentences.en: Health-care organizations should furnish guidance for informed-consent protocols that respond to the new types of risk inherent in AI-driven treatment, and providers should discuss these risks with patients.
sentences.zh: 医疗保健组织应为应对人工智能驱动治疗中固有的新型风险的知情同意方案提供指导，并且提供者应与患者讨论这些风险。

blocks.html_en: With these systems, physicians can be criticised for enrolling an unsuitable patient, failing to respond to device alarms or not understanding system limitations. Organizations might be judged on how they selected, validated and monitored the technology. Manufacturers might be liable if flawed designs or updates contribute to harm. But conventional liability assessments can be unfit for purpose, if physicians and organizations acted reasonably, and harm is caused by an algorithmically determined decision that is not obviously wrong.

sentences.en: With these systems, physicians can be criticised for enrolling an unsuitable patient, failing to respond to device alarms or not understanding system limitations.
sentences.zh: 使用这些系统，医生可能会因招募不合适的患者、未能响应设备警报或不了解系统限制而受到批评。

sentences.en: Organizations might be judged on how they selected, validated and monitored the technology.
sentences.zh: 人们可能会根据组织如何选择、验证和监控技术来对其进行评判。

sentences.en: Manufacturers might be liable if flawed designs or updates contribute to harm.
sentences.zh: 如果有缺陷的设计或更新造成损害，制造商可能要承担责任。

sentences.en: But conventional liability assessments can be unfit for purpose, if physicians and organizations acted reasonably, and harm is caused by an algorithmically determined decision that is not obviously wrong.
sentences.zh: 但如果医生和组织采取合理行动，传统的责任评估可能无法达到目的，并且由算法确定的决策造成的伤害并不是明显错误的。

blocks.html_en: Level 4: AI-triggered human oversight. AI tools with moderate-to-high levels of autonomy and automation, and broad operational scope. These systems manage whole episodes of therapy in areas such as intensive care. They continuously monitor patients and adjust treatments — for instance balancing ventilator and sedation settings against several physiological targets at once. They trigger back-up protocols such as summoning a rapid-response team when something seems wrong. Clinicians are a safety net and act only when the system sounds the alarm. Level 4 deployments are yet to break through in medicine, although the technical components needed are emerging.

sentences.en: Level 4: AI-triggered human oversight.
sentences.zh: 第四级：人工智能引发的人类监督。

sentences.en: AI tools with moderate-to-high levels of autonomy and automation, and broad operational scope.
sentences.zh: 具有中高级自主性和自动化程度、操作范围广泛的人工智能工具。

sentences.en: These systems manage whole episodes of therapy in areas such as intensive care.
sentences.zh: 这些系统管理重症监护等领域的整个治疗过程。

sentences.en: They continuously monitor patients and adjust treatments — for instance balancing ventilator and sedation settings against several physiological targets at once.
sentences.zh: 他们持续监测患者并调整治疗，例如根据多个生理目标同时平衡呼吸机和镇静设置。

sentences.en: They trigger back-up protocols such as summoning a rapid-response team when something seems wrong.
sentences.zh: 当出现问题时，它们会触发后备协议，例如召集快速响应团队。

sentences.en: Clinicians are a safety net and act only when the system sounds the alarm.
sentences.zh: 临床医生是一张安全网，只有在系统发出警报时才会采取行动。

sentences.en: Level 4 deployments are yet to break through in medicine, although the technical components needed are emerging.
sentences.zh: 尽管所需的技术组件正在出现，但 4 级部署在医学领域尚未取得突破。

blocks.html_en: For these systems, regulators should require strong evidence that including a human in the loop would reduce safety. Given that clinicians would have no realistic opportunity to review the actions of these systems, courts might struggle to determine whether an adverse outcome reflects negligence, a hidden defect or simply the inherent risks of medicine.

sentences.en: For these systems, regulators should require strong evidence that including a human in the loop would reduce safety.
sentences.zh: 对于这些系统，监管机构应该要求强有力的证据证明，将人纳入回路会降低安全性。

sentences.en: Given that clinicians would have no realistic opportunity to review the actions of these systems, courts might struggle to determine whether an adverse outcome reflects negligence, a hidden defect or simply the inherent risks of medicine.
sentences.zh: 鉴于临床医生没有现实的机会来审查这些系统的行为，法院可能很难确定不良结果是否反映了疏忽、隐藏的缺陷或仅仅是医学的固有风险。

blocks.html_en: Generative AI could revolutionize health care — but not if control is ceded to big tech

sentences.en: Generative AI could revolutionize health care — but not if control is ceded to big tech
sentences.zh: 生成式人工智能可能会彻底改变医疗保健——但如果控制权被让给大型科技公司，情况就不会如此

content_html_zh:
人工智能正在迅速融入医院和医疗诊所。 然而，人工智能工具带来的好处也带来了新的患者安全风险，以及出现问题时谁负责的问题。

按照惯例，医疗保健方面的责任是明确界定的。 临床医生必须提供一套治疗标准。 机构必须组织安全的治疗流程。 制造商必须提供无缺陷的医疗设备。 如果其中任何一方未达到预期标准，涉及许可和证书的监管机构和机构可以进行干预。 如果患者受到伤害，法院可以评估哪一方应承担责任。

医疗人工智能工具的到来将模糊这些界限。

当前的人工智能工具主要用作助手，并由人工检查支持，就像其他医疗设备一样。 例如，当人工智能模型触发患者有败血症风险的警报时，临床医生必须在进行任何治疗之前审查并确认生理原理。

医疗人工智能可以改变医学——但前提是我们仔细跟踪它所接触的数据

但在接下来的几年里，人工智能驱动的临床工具预计将从合成数据发展到对数据采取行动，而人类的输入会越来越少。 他们将进行诊断、制定治疗计划并做出临床医生很少或根本不参与的患者管理决策。 尽管许多现有工具的输出是可以理解的——例如败血症模型，通过根据透明公式组合定义的生理变量来工作——更先进的工具可以涉及黑盒深度学习过程。 临床医生将不再能够完全遵循工具的推理，即使算法为他们的判断提供了一些解释2。

这些工具介于问责规则之间。 他们的黑箱推理使得很难确定他们何时存在缺陷。 当人类和不透明的人工智能模型共同做出决策时，当人们在接受医疗保健时受到伤害时，就很难评估责任。 现有的医疗责任框架没有解决这个交叉点3。

这种法律上的不确定性意味着受到伤害的人可能会陷入责任空白，而没有人明确违反规则3。 由于担心法律风险，医院可能会避免使用人工智能来实现潜在有用的功能——医生们一再将这种担忧视为安全采用人工智能的障碍4-6，并且一些人认为这是不使用现有黑盒工具的理由。 一旦工具进入市场，人工智能供应商可能会逃避监控安全的义务，因为他们相信，当出现问题时，很难将责任归咎于他们。

需要明确的责任框架。

在这里，我们概述了如何实现这一目标，根据三个因素定义七个级别的人工智能能力：自主性、自动化和操作范围。 对于飞机和自动驾驶汽车，监管机构已经使用分级来准确指定系统必须执行哪些任务、如何独立以及何时预计人类接管7-9。 医疗人工智能系统的类似级别将帮助监管机构、政策制定者、政府、法院和专业医疗机构规划即将到来的工具。

三个属性，七个级别

三个属性决定了人工智能在临床中的使用方式。

第一，自主性：系统如何独立推理，而不需要人工输入。 现有的脓毒症风险模型是低自主性的人工智能工具1。 相比之下，深度学习系统可能会根据数千个变量的模式得出诊断，并做出医生无法追溯的推论10。

其次，自动化：医疗人工智能系统可以自行执行哪些任务。 这样的系统可能包括从外科医生控制的低自动化机器人到直接将化疗处方发送到药房的系统。

第三，运行范围：允许系统运行的边界。 与初级保健诊所使用的用于自主决定是否将患者转诊给专家的相同工具相比，专业眼科服务机构部署的用于复核临床决策的视网膜成像系统的风险较小。

以下七个级别可以构成定义医疗人工智能工具风险的基础。 给定的工具可能处于不同的级别，具体取决于它的使用地点、方式以及使用者。

0 级：信息性。 没有自主性、自动化程度可变、操作范围狭窄的人工智能系统。 此类系统根据人类设定的规则存储、移动和显示数据。 例子包括管理电子健康记录的算法或来自跟踪生命体征的可穿戴设备的流数据。 算法行为是透明的，任何输出都是可独立验证的。

这是人们常去的地方。 监管机构可以评估此​​类工具是否可靠并提供足够的网络安全和数据保护。 法院可以应用传统标准来评估责任。

1 级：辅助。 自主性低、自动化程度低到中等、操作范围窄的人工智能系统。 此类系统可以在临床医生的监督下执行单一、明确定义的任务，例如在心脏监护仪上标记可疑心律11或在扫描上突出显示可能的肺结节12。 这些工具的算法推理可能是不透明的，但可以通过对患者数据的临床审查或通过检查模型输入和输出数据之间的相关性的“可解释性技术”来验证输出。

这些工具作为诊断辅助工具受到监管，类似于现有的乳房X光检查和结肠镜检查计算机辅助检测系统。 医院有责任确保工作人员了解其局限性。 用户应该准确判断警报是否有意义。

训练临床人工智能像医生团队一样进行推理

第 2 级：决策支持。 自主性低、自动化程度低到中等、操作范围适中的人工智能工具。 这些系统结合了多个数据流——可能包括症状、既往病史、影像数据和当前指南。 此级别的现有工具可以制定诊断和治疗计划，起草详细的出院摘要并生成分诊决策的风险评分。 与 1 级工具一样，它们被设计为咨询性的——它们的推理可能不透明，但在某种程度上是可验证的，临床医生应该做出最终决定。

监管机构应要求提供强有力的证据来证明这些系统改善了护理。 医院必须培训临床医生质疑输出结果，而不是默认接受它们，法院必须决定临床医生在这种情况下对特定建议的依赖是否合理。 临床医生在时间压力下可能会过度依赖咨询工具。 没有简单的方法可以确定临床医生在多大程度上受到机器建议的影响。

第 3 级：监督自动化。 具有中等自主性和自动化水平、中等操作范围的人工智能系统。 决策者是系统，而不是临床医生。 这些工具目前很少见（参见“当前医疗人工智能的分类”）。 在严格定义的领域中，它们可以动态响应治疗需求 - 例如，胰岛素输送设备使用嵌入式算法和预定义的限制，根据连续血糖读数自动调整剂量13。 临床医生选择将哪些患者置于系统中，并仅在出现问题时进行干预。

监管机构应重点关注使用和维护这些系统的说明的质量以及有关提供护理所固有风险的信息。 医疗保健组织应为应对人工智能驱动治疗中固有的新型风险的知情同意方案提供指导，并且提供者应与患者讨论这些风险。

使用这些系统，医生可能会因招募不合适的患者、未能响应设备警报或不了解系统限制而受到批评。 人们可能会根据组织如何选择、验证和监控技术来对其进行评判。 如果有缺陷的设计或更新造成损害，制造商可能要承担责任。 但如果医生和组织采取合理行动，传统的责任评估可能无法达到目的，并且由算法确定的决策造成的伤害并不是明显错误的。

第四级：人工智能引发的人类监督。 具有中高级自主性和自动化程度、操作范围广泛的人工智能工具。 这些系统管理重症监护等领域的整个治疗过程。 他们持续监测患者并调整治疗，例如根据多个生理目标同时平衡呼吸机和镇静设置。 当出现问题时，它们会触发后备协议，例如召集快速响应团队。 临床医生是一张安全网，只有在系统发出警报时才会采取行动。 尽管所需的技术组件正在出现，但 4 级部署在医学领域尚未取得突破。

对于这些系统，监管机构应该要求强有力的证据证明，将人纳入回路会降低安全性。 鉴于临床医生没有现实的机会来审查这些系统的行为，法院可能很难确定不良结果是否反映了疏忽、隐藏的缺陷或仅仅是医学的固有风险。

生成式人工智能可能会彻底改变医疗保健——但如果控制权被让给大型科技公司，情况就不会如此
